paragraphs.text: The divine Word sets before us a teaching on prayer. Through the words of the prayer he shows his worthy disciples, those who earnestly seek to know how to pray, how they should win God's hearing. But I would venture to add a little to what is written. This present assembly needs to be taught not how one ought to pray, but that one ought to pray at all, which is something most people have perhaps never yet heard. In everyday life most people neglect and set aside this sacred and divine work of prayer. So it seems right to me first to declare, as well as I can, that we must persevere in prayer without fail, as the Apostle says, and only then to listen to the divine voice that teaches us how we should bring our petition to the Lord. For I see that in this present life everything else is pursued more eagerly. One person's soul is turned to one thing, another's to something else, but people are not eager for the good of prayer. The shopkeeper is at his business before dawn. He competes to show his goods to buyers before his fellow tradesmen do, so that he can meet the customer's need first, get ahead of the others and sell his own wares. In the same way the buyer is afraid that someone else will get there first and he will miss what he needs, so he runs to the market and not to the house of prayer. And since everyone has the same desire for gain and competes to get ahead of his neighbour, these pursuits steal the hour of prayer away and hand it over to trade. So it is with the craftsman, and so with the man

whose business is with words. So it is with the litigant and with the man appointed to judge. Each one leans wholly and eagerly toward the business in hand and has forgotten the work of prayer, for he thinks that time given to God is a loss to his own purpose. The man who practises a trade thinks that God's help with his task is an idle and useless thing. So he abandons prayer and puts his hopes in his hands, forgetting the One who gave him hands. In the same way, the man who works hard to master eloquence does not consider the One who gave him speech. As if he had brought himself into being with this nature, he gives his attention to himself and to his pupils' studies. He supposes that none of his good things will come to him from God's working, and so he values study above prayer. In the same way all other pursuits crowd out the soul's concern with greater and heavenly things through anxiety over bodily and earthly ones. That is why there is so much sin in life, always growing larger as it is added to and entangled in every human pursuit. Forgetfulness of God has gained control of everything, and people do not join the good of prayer to the things they pursue. Greed comes in along with trade, and greed is idolatry. So too the farmer does not measure his farming by his real needs. He keeps stretching his efforts toward more, and by spreading out into what belongs to others he gives sin wide entry into his occupation. From this spring quarrels that are hard to heal, as men gripped by the same disease of greed rise up against one another over the boundaries of their land. From this come fits of rage, impulses toward evil and attacks on one another, which often end in bloodshed and murder. Likewise the business of the law courts serves sins of every kind and finds countless ways to plead for injustice. Either the judge willingly tilts the scales of justice toward a bribe, or, against his will, he is deceived by the cunning of those who confuse the truth and ratifies injustice. Why list one by one all the ways in which sin, in its many branches and forms, mixes itself into human life? Its cause is simply this: people do not enlist God's help in the business they have in hand. If prayer comes before our work, sin will find no way into the soul. For when the remembrance of God is settled in the heart, the schemes of the adversary come to nothing, and justice acts as mediator in every dispute. Prayer also keeps the farmer from sin, because it makes a small plot of land yield an abundant harvest, so that no longer, along with the desire for more, does there enter

sin. So it is with the traveller, and so with the man who sets out for war or for marriage. So it is with anyone at all who is bent on some undertaking. If he does each thing with prayer, the success of his undertaking will turn him away from sin, since nothing hostile drags his soul down into passion. But if he turns away from God and gives himself wholly to his pursuit, then whoever is outside God must necessarily be on the opposing side. Whoever does not join himself to God through prayer is separated from God. This, then, is what our discourse must teach us first: that we ought always to pray and not lose heart. For prayer brings us to be with God, and whoever is with God is separated from the adversary.

Prayer is the safeguard of self-control, the schooling of anger, the curbing of arrogance, the cleansing of grudges, the overthrow of envy, the removal of injustice and the correction of impiety. Prayer is strength to bodies, prosperity to a household, good order to a city, power to a kingdom, a trophy in war and security in peace. It reconciles those who are divided and keeps those who are united together. Prayer is the seal of virginity, the faithfulness of marriage, a weapon for travellers, a guard for those who sleep, courage for those who keep watch, a good harvest for farmers and safety for seafarers. Prayer is an advocate for those on trial, release for prisoners, rest for the weary, consolation for the grieving, delight for the joyful, comfort for mourners, a crown for those who marry, a feast on birthdays and a shroud for the dying. Prayer is conversation with God and contemplation of the invisible. It gives full assurance to those who long for it and equal honour with the angels. It advances what is good, overthrows what is evil and corrects sinners. It is the enjoyment of things present and the substance of things to come. Prayer made the sea monster a home for Jonah. It brought Hezekiah back to life from the very gates of death. It turned the flame into a dewy breeze for the three young men. It set up a trophy for the Israelites over the Amalekites. In a single night and with an invisible sword it laid low a hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians. Countless other examples besides can be found in past events, and they make it clear that nothing of value in this life ranks higher than prayer.

But it is time now to turn to the prayer itself. Or rather, let us first add a little more to what we have said. We have received many good things of every kind from God's grace, and we have only one thing to give in return for what we have received: to repay our Benefactor with prayer and thanksgiving. Yet I reckon that even if we spent our whole life in conversation with God, giving thanks and praying, we would still fall as far short of a worthy return as if we had never even wanted to repay our Benefactor at all. In three divisions

the span of time is measured: past, present and future, and in all three the Lord's kindness is found. If you consider the present, it is in him that you live. If you consider the future, he is your hope of what you expect. If you consider the past, you would not have existed before he made you. You were blessed when you received your very existence from him. Once you existed you were blessed again, living and moving in him, as the Apostle says. And our hopes for what is to come depend on the same working of his. You, however, are master only of the present. So even if you never stopped thanking God at every moment, you would barely pay your debt of gratitude for the present. You would find no way at all to repay what you owe for the future or the past. Yet we fall far short even of the thanksgiving that is within our power. We do not show gratitude even as far as we can. I do not say for the whole day; we do not set aside even the smallest part of the day for time with God. Who spread out the earth beneath me? Who by his wisdom made the waters something one can travel across? Who set the sky over me like a vault? Who carries the torch of the sun for me? Who sends springs into the valleys? Who prepared channels for the rivers? Who yoked the irrational animals to my service? Who made me, lifeless dust, share in life and understanding? Who shaped this clay in the image of the divine likeness? When sin had defaced the divine image in me, who restored it to its original grace? I was exiled from paradise, shut out from the tree of life and buried in the pit of material life: who draws me back to my first blessedness? "There is none who understands," says Scripture. For if we really looked at these things, we would give thanks without end and without ceasing all our lives long. But as it is, almost the whole of human nature is awake only to material things. These are what we strive for and are eager about, and our memory and hope are taken up with them. Human nature never sleeps or rests in its desire for more, in anything at all where more can be found. Whether in honour and glory, in abundance of wealth or in the disease of anger, our nature always looks for more. But the true goods of God, both those we see and those that are promised, count for nothing.

But it is time also to consider, as far as we can, the meaning of the words of the prayer. For clearly we obtain what we want by learning how we ought to ask for it. What, then, is the teaching? "When you pray," he says, "do not babble like the gentiles, for they think they will be heard because of their many words." Perhaps the meaning of this teaching is already clear from these words, since it is set out for us

quite plainly and needs no subtler examination. Still, it is worth asking what the word "babble" (battologia) means, so that once we have learned its sense we may keep clear of what is forbidden. It seems to me that he is rebuking slackness of mind and restraining those who are sunk in vain desires. That is why he coined this strange new word, to expose the folly of those whose desires pour out over useless and empty things. For speech that is sensible and intelligent and looks to what is useful is properly called speech (logos). But speech that pours itself out on unreal desires, for the sake of a pleasure that has no substance, is not logos but battologia. Putting the idea in more ordinary Greek, one might call it prattle, nonsense, drivel, or any other word with that kind of meaning. What, then, does the Word advise us? Not to fall, at the time of prayer, into the state of mind of little children. Immature minds do not think about how anything they want might actually come about. Instead they make up good fortune for themselves as they please. They imagine treasures and kingdoms and great cities named after them, and in their minds they become whatever the vanity of their thoughts sketches for them. Some carry this vanity further still and overstep the limits of nature. They grow wings, or shine like the stars, or carry mountains in their hands, or build themselves a road to heaven, or live to their ten-thousandth year, becoming young again after being old. The heart of the more childish produces these and other such inventions, empty as bubbles. In practical affairs, a man who does not think about how his plans might bring about some good, but busies himself with unreal desires, is foolish and wretched, because he wastes on these dreams the time he should spend planning something useful. In the same way, a man who at the time of prayer is not intent on what benefits the soul, but expects God to fall in with the passionate impulses of his mind, is truly a speaker of nonsense and a babbler. He is praying for God to become the accomplice and servant of his own vanities. Here is what I mean. Someone comes to God in prayer without having considered how lofty the Power is that he approaches, and without realising it he insults God's greatness with shameful and petty requests. Imagine someone who, through extreme poverty or ignorance, prized earthenware pots. He comes before a king who is minded to hand out riches and honours, but he passes over the requests fit for a king and asks one of such great dignity to mould some clay and make something to his liking. So too the man who prays in an ignorant way does not raise himself to the height of the Giver. He wants the divine power to come down to the low and earthly level of his own desire. For this reason he lays his passionate impulses before the One who sees into hearts, not so that God may heal these perverse

impulses of his mind, but so that they may grow worse, as the evil impulse is carried into action with God's cooperation. For since so-and-so is troubling me and my heart is set against him, the man says to God, "Strike him!" He all but cries out, "Let my passion arise in you; let my wickedness pass over to you." In human fights no one can fight on one side without sharing the angry man's rage against his opponent. In the same way, whoever stirs God up against his enemy is clearly asking him to share his anger and become a partner in his wrath. But this would mean that the Divine falls into passion, is disposed as a human being is, and is changed from its good nature into the cruelty of a beast. So it is with the man mad for glory, and so with the man who in his arrogance wants more than others. So it is with the man eager to win his lawsuit, the man pressing toward the crown in the athletic games and the man striving for applause in the theatres. Often it is so too with the man wasted by the raging passion of youth. All of these bring their petitions to God not to be freed from the sickness that rules them, but so that their disease may reach its goal. Each of them regards failure in these things as a disaster, and so they really are babbling, begging God to become an accomplice in the sickness of their minds. Worst of all, they want the Divine to be moved by contrary impulses, and they divide God's working between savagery and kindness. The very One whom they want to be merciful and gentle toward themselves, they ask to show himself bitter and harsh toward their enemies. Oh, the folly of the babblers! If God is harsh toward them, he is certainly not gentle toward you either. And if, as you hope, he inclines toward mercy in your case, how could he turn the other way and change his mercy into bitterness? But the contentious have an objection to this ready to hand. They at once cite the words of the prophets in defence of their own bitterness. David longs for sinners to perish and prays that shame and disgrace may fall on his enemies. Jeremiah longs to see God's vengeance on his adversaries. Hosea asks that his enemies be given a childless womb and dry breasts. They collect many such passages scattered through the holy Scriptures to argue that we ought to curse our adversaries, and that God's goodness should become the accomplice of their own bitterness. But in passing we shall put a stop to the babbling of those whom such texts lead the wrong way, and so we shall set out the following about each of the passages mentioned.

The truly holy, who were moved by God through the Holy Spirit and whose sayings were written down by God's providence to admonish those who came after them, will never be shown to have been eager for anything evil. The whole aim of their words is to correct the wickedness that has made its home in our nature. A man who prays that there may be no sick and no poor does not want the people themselves to be destroyed, but sickness and poverty to disappear. In the same way, each of the saints prays for the destruction of what is hostile and inimical to our nature. Yet this gives the less educated the impression that the saints are bitter and angry with human beings. When the Psalmist says, "Let sinners and the lawless perish from the earth, so that they are no more," he is praying for sin and lawlessness to perish. For a human being is not the enemy of other human beings. It is the will's movement toward evil that has turned into an enemy what is joined to us by nature. So he prays for evil to perish; but a human being is not evil, for how could the likeness of the Good be evil? So too when he prays for shame and disgrace on his enemies, he is pointing you to the host of adversaries who come from the invisible enemy to make war on human life. Paul describes them more plainly when he says that our struggle is against the principalities, against the powers and the rulers of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. The demons lay plots that bring people evil occasions for sin: fits of anger, triggers of desire, and the roots of envy, hatred, pride and other such evils. The great Prophet sees these plots prowling around every soul, and when he prays against these enemies he prays that they may come to shame. And this means praying for his own salvation. For it is natural that the one who is beaten in wrestling should be ashamed of his fall, just as the winner rejoices in his victory. The form of the prayer shows that this is so: "Let those who seek my soul," he says, "be put to shame and disgraced." He does not curse those who plot to damage his property, or who quarrel over the boundaries of his land, or who show some malice against his body. He curses those who plot against his soul. And what plot against the soul is there other than estrangement from God? The only thing that estranges a human soul from God is a disposition ruled by passion. Since the Divine is always free from passion, whoever is always caught up in passion is cut off from union with the Divine. So that this may not happen to him, he prays that his opponents in the struggle may be put to shame. This is nothing other than praying for his own victory over his enemies, and those enemies are the passions. In the same way Jeremiah had zeal for true religion at a time when the king was mad for idols and his subjects had been corrupted along with him. He is not indulging some passion of his own; rather, concerning the common

…offers the prayer [?] against those who had acted impiously, asking that the whole human race be brought to its senses. In the same way the prophet, seeing wickedness multiplying among the Israelites, rightly condemns it to childlessness and wishes the bitter breasts of sin to dry up, so that evil might neither be born among people nor nourished. That is why the prophet says, “Give them, Lord, a childless womb and dry breasts.” And if any other saying of this kind is found among the saints, one that carries some charge and sign of anger, it always looks to this meaning: that it should banish the evil, not crush the human being. “God did not make death.” Do you hear the declaration? How then could the saint have appealed to God for death against his own enemies, when God is a stranger to the working of death and takes no delight in the destruction of the living? But the one who babbles, and stirs up God's love for humankind against his own enemies, is urging him to take delight in human misfortunes. “But some people,” someone says, “have already gained offices and honours and wealth by using prayer for this, and because of such good fortune they were thought to be dear to God.” How then, one might ask, can you forbid us to bring our petitions to God about such things? Well, that everything depends on the divine will, and that life here below is ordered from above, is plain to everyone, and no one could contradict it. But we have learned other reasons for such successes of prayer. It is not that God grants these things to those who ask as though they were good in every respect. It is so that through them faith in God may be strengthened in the more superficial, and so that we, learning little by little by experience in our smaller requests that God hears our supplications, may at some point rise to the desire for lofty gifts worthy of God. We see this with our own children. For a while they cling to the mother's breast, seeking from the one who bore them as much as their nature can hold. But once the infant has grown a little and gained some power of speech, it scorns the breast and looks for something like a necklace [?], or a garment, or other such things that delight the eyes of little children. And when it comes of age, and the mind has grown together with the body, then it leaves behind all childish desires and will ask its parents for things that serve a grown-up life. In the same way God, accustoming man to look to him in all things, for this reason often does not refuse to hear even the smaller requests, so that by his kindness in small things he may call the one who has received the favour to desire loftier things. So you too: if so-and-so has by divine providence risen from obscurity to become well known and admired, or has gained some other of the things people seek in this life, office

or wealth, or renown, understand [?] that his kindness in these matters is a demonstration of God's great power, so that, having received childish toys, you may bring the Father your requests about greater and loftier [?] things. [?] are those things that bring profit to the soul. For it would be the height of absurdity to come before God and ask the Eternal for temporal things, the Heavenly for earthly things, the Most High for lowly things, the one who bestows [?] the kingdom of heaven for this earthly and humble good fortune, the one who grants gifts that cannot be taken away for the brief use of things that belong to others: things whose loss [?] is inevitable, whose enjoyment is short-lived, and whose management is dangerous. And he makes this clear well by adding, “as the Gentiles do.” For to be eager about things that do not last is the mark of those who suppose for themselves no hope of the age to come, no [?] fear of judgment, no threat of Gehenna, no expectation [?], nor anything else that is hoped for according to [Scripture?]. Like cattle, they look only to the present life, and count among the goods whatever gratifies the throat and the belly and the other pleasures of the body, or being first among some and being thought above the rest, or sleeping on a pile of talents, or whatever else belongs to the deceit of this world. If anyone speaks to them of the hope to come, he seems [?] to be talking sheer nonsense when he describes paradise and the kingdom and the life of the heavens, or goes through such things. Since, then, it is the mark of those who have no hope to cling to the present life, he rightly says that the superfluous and vain objects of desire, which pleasure-lovers think they can secure for themselves by prayer, belong to the Gentiles, who [suppose] that by pestering God about absurd things they will draw the Divine toward what is not fitting. “They think,” he says, “that they will be heard for their many words.” These are the things one must know, and we have examined [?] and been taught them. What kind of prayer we ought to offer [to God] we shall learn [?] in what follows, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the might to the ages of ages.

Our Father who art in heaven. When the great Moses brought the people of Israel to the initiation at the mountain, he did not count them worthy of the manifestation of God until he had laid down for them a law of purification by chastity and sprinkling. Even so, they did not dare to face the appearance of the divine power, but were terrified at everything that happened: the fire, the darkness, the smoke, the [trumpets?]. And turning away from these again, they [begged] the lawgiver to become a mediator for them of the divine

[word?], since their own power was not enough to draw near to God and receive a divine manifestation. But our lawgiver, our Lord Jesus Christ, when he was about to bring us to the divine grace, does not show us in his teaching a Mount Sinai covered in darkness and smoking with fire, or trumpet blasts sounding something indistinct and terrifying. He does not purify the soul with three days of abstinence and with water that washes off dirt, nor does he leave the whole assembly at the foot of the mountain and grant to one man alone the ascent to the summit, which was covered by the darkness that hid the glory of God. Instead, first of all, in place of the mountain he leads us up to heaven itself, having made it accessible to human beings through virtue. Then he makes those who come to him not only spectators of the divine power but also sharers in it, and in a certain way leads them into kinship with the nature that is above all things. Nor does he hide the surpassing glory in darkness, as though it were hard for those who seek it to see, but having lit up the darkness with the far-shining light of his teaching, he has made the ineffable glory visible, in bright clear air, to the pure in heart. And as for water for sprinkling, he grants it not from foreign streams but from what wells up within ourselves, whether one means the fountains of the eyes or the pure conscience of the heart. And he lays down a law of abstinence not from some defilement in the lawful union of married people, but from every material and passionate disposition; and so he brings us to God through prayer. For this is the force of the words: through them we learn from the passage not certain sounds uttered in syllables, but the idea of the ascent to God that is achieved through a lofty way of life. It is possible to grasp the divine initiation through the very words of the prayer. “When you pray,” he says. He did not say, “When you vow,” but “When you pray,” since what belongs to the vow ought already to have been accomplished before one draws near to God through prayer. What is the difference in meaning between these words? A vow is a promise of something dedicated in piety, whereas prayer is a request for good things brought to God with supplication. Since, then, we need boldness when we come before God making requests for what is profitable, the vow must necessarily lead the way, so that, having fulfilled our own part, we may then confidently expect to receive what comes from God. That is why the prophet says, “I will pay you my vows, which my lips uttered,” and, “Make vows, and pay them to the Lord our God.” In many places of Scripture one can see the word “vow” used in this sense, so that we know that a vow is, as has been said, a promise of thank-offerings, while prayer

signifies the approach to God that is made after the promise has been fulfilled. The passage therefore teaches us not to ask anything of God before we have brought him as a gift something pleasing to him. For first comes the vow, then the prayer, just as if one were to say that sowing comes before the harvest. So we must first sow the seeds of the vow, and then, once they have grown [?], those who have sown the seeds receive the grace by reaping it through prayer. Since, then, the encounter will not be in boldness unless the approach follows upon some vow and offering made beforehand, the vow must necessarily precede the prayer. As though this had already been accomplished, then, the Lord says to his disciples, “When you pray, say: Our Father who art in heaven.” “Who will give me wings like a dove?” the great David says somewhere in the Psalms. I too would say, borrowing [?] the same words: Who will give me those wings, so that I may fly up in thought to the height of the grandeur of these words? So that I might leave the whole earth behind and pass through all the air spread out between, reach the beauty of the ether, arrive at the stars and behold all their ordered array; and not stop even there, but pass through them too and come to be outside everything that moves and changes, and grasp the nature that stands firm, the unmoved [?] power that is established in itself, which leads and carries all things that exist, all of them depending on the ineffable will of the divine [power?]. So that, having gone far in thought from everything that alters and changes, in a soul unchanging and unwavering, I might first make the unchanging and unalterable one my own by my disposition, and only then call upon him by the most intimate [name] and say, “Father.” What kind of soul does one need to say this! How much boldness, what a conscience! One would first have to understand God as far as possible, being led by the hand through the names by which he is conceived toward some grasp of the ineffable glory, and learn that the divine nature, whatever it is in itself, is goodness, holiness, joy, power, glory [?], purity, eternity, always the same and in the same state; and to grasp all such things as are understood about the divine nature, both through the divine Scripture and through one's own reasoning. Will he then dare to utter such a word and call such a being his father? For it is clear that if he has any sense, he would not dare, unless he sees the same qualities in himself, to address that word to God and say, “Father.” For the one who is good by essence cannot become the father of a wicked deed; nor can the [Holy One?] be father of one whose life has been profaned,

nor the Unchangeable of one who keeps turning about, nor the Father of life of one made a corpse by sin, nor the Pure and Undefiled of those who disgrace themselves in shameful passions, nor the Benefactor of the greedy, nor, in a word, the one who is seen in every good of those who are found in any evil. For if someone who, looking at himself, still needs cleansing, and who recognizes that his conscience is foul, full of stains and evil brands, should, before he is cleansed of such great evils, adopt himself into kinship with God and say “Father,” the unjust to the Just, the unclean to the Pure, his words would be sheer insolence and abuse, since he would be naming God the father of his own wickedness. For the word “father” signifies the cause of what has come into being from him. So the man with a foul conscience, if he calls God his father, will be doing nothing other than accusing him of being the originator and cause of his own evils. “But what fellowship has light with darkness?” says the Apostle. Rather, light is akin to light, the just to the just, the beautiful to the beautiful, the incorruptible to the incorruptible, and opposites are always related to what is of their own kind. For “a good tree cannot bear bad fruit.” If, then, someone is “heavy of heart,” as Scripture says, and “seeks falsehood,” and yet ventures to use the words of the prayer, let him know that such a person is calling not on the heavenly Father but on the infernal one, who is himself a liar and becomes the father of the lie that takes shape in each person; he is sin and the father of sin. That is why those whose souls are given over to the passions are called “children of wrath” by the Apostle, and he who has fallen away from life is named “son of perdition,” and a certain sluggish and effeminate man was called “son of runaway girls.” Likewise, on the opposite side, those whose conscience is bright are called “sons of light and of day,” and others, who have strengthened themselves toward the divine might, are called “sons of power.” So when the Lord teaches us in prayer to call God Father, he seems to me to be doing nothing other than laying down the law of a lofty and exalted [?] life. For the Truth certainly does not teach us to lie, to say what we are not and to name what we are not by nature. Rather, in calling the incorruptible, just and good one our Father, we are to prove the kinship true by our life. Do you see how much preparation we need? What kind of life? How much zeal, and of what kind, so that our conscience may at last be raised to this measure of boldness and we may dare to say to God, “Father”? For if your eyes are on money, if you are taken up with the deceit of this life, or seek glory from people, if you are a slave to the more passionate desires, and then take such a prayer on your lips, what do you think he who looks into your life and hears your prayer will say? I seem to hear words like these, as though God were saying to such a person:

“You whose life is corrupt, do you call the Father of incorruption your Father? Why do you defile the undefiled name with your filthy voice? Why do you make a lie of the word? Why do you insult the stainless nature? If you were my child, your life too would surely bear the stamp of my goods. I do not recognize the image of my nature in you; your features are those of the opposite. What fellowship has light with darkness? What kinship has life with death? What affinity has the one who is pure by nature with the impure? Great is the gap between the benefactor and the greedy. The merciful and the cruel are opposites that cannot mix. The evils in you have another father, for my offspring are adorned with their father's goods: the merciful is the child of the Merciful, and the pure of the Pure; corruption is foreign to the Incorruptible; and in short, the good come from the Good and the just from the Just. But as for you, I do not know where you come from.” It is dangerous, therefore, to venture on the [words?] of the prayer before one's life has been cleansed, and to name God one's Father. But let us hear the words of the prayer again, in case by repeating them more often we may come to understand their hidden meaning. Our Father who art in heaven. That we must make God our own by a life of virtue has been examined well enough in what we said before. But the passage seems to me to hint at a deeper meaning as well. For these words remind us of the homeland from which we have fallen and the noble birth that we have lost. In the story of the young man who left his father's hearth and deserted to a swinish life, the Word shows human wretchedness by narrating his departure and his prodigal living. And he does not bring him back to his original good fortune until the young man has become aware of his present misery, come to himself, and rehearsed the words of repentance. Those words somehow agreed with the words of the prayer, for he said there, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.” He would not have added the sin against heaven to his confession unless he had been convinced that heaven was the homeland he had sinned by leaving. That is why rehearsing such a confession makes the father approachable to him, so that the father runs to him and greets his neck with a kiss. This signifies the yoke of the word, laid on man through the mouth by the tradition of the gospel, on him who had cast off the first yoke of the commandment and shaken off the law that protected him. And the father puts the robe on him, not another one but the first, of which he had been stripped through disobedience when, as soon as he tasted what was forbidden, he saw that he was naked. And the ring on his hand, with the engraving on its bezel, signifies the recovery of the

image. He also protects his feet with sandals, so that he may not come near the serpent's head with a bare heel and fall victim to its bite. Just as there the young man's return to his father's hearth became the cause of his father's kindness to him (and this hearth is heaven, against which he tells his father he has sinned), so here too, it seems to me, the Lord, in teaching you to call on the Father in heaven, is making you remember your good homeland, so that, by instilling in you a stronger desire for good things, he may set you on the road that leads back again to that homeland. And the road that leads human nature up to heaven is none other than flight and withdrawal from earthly evils; and the means of fleeing evils seems to me to be nothing other than becoming like God. To become like God is to become just and holy and good, and the like. If anyone clearly imprints the features of these things on himself, as far as possible, he will pass without toil, of his own accord, from earthly life to the heavenly realm. For God's distance from humankind is not a matter of place, as though we needed some device or contrivance to move this heavy, weighty, earthy flesh to a bodiless and spiritual mode of life. Rather, since virtue is separated from evil in the realm of the mind, it lies in man's free choice alone to be in whichever of the two he inclines toward by his desire. Since, then, no toil follows upon choosing the good (and attaining what one has chosen follows upon choosing it), you can be in heaven at once, once you have received God into your mind. For if, as Ecclesiastes says, “God is in heaven,” and you, as the Prophet says, “have clung to God,” then it is absolutely necessary that the one joined to God should be where God is. So in commanding us in prayer to call God our own Father, he is bidding you to do nothing other than become like the heavenly Father by a way of life worthy of God, just as he enjoins this more plainly elsewhere when he says, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” If, then, we have understood the meaning of this prayer, it is time to prepare our souls, so that we may at last dare to take these words on our lips and say with boldness, “Our Father who art in heaven.” For just as the marks of likeness to God are plain, through which a person can become a child of God (“For as many as received him,” it says, “to them he gave power to become children of God,” and the one who receives God into himself is the one who has taken up perfection in the good), so too there are distinctive signs of the evil character, and anyone found in them cannot be a son of God, since he bears the image of the opposite nature. Do you want to know the properties of the evil character? Envy, hatred, slander, pride, greed, passionate

…desire, the [?] that goes with a mad craving for glory: these and things like them are what mark out the form of the adversary. So if someone whose soul is branded with stains like these calls on a "Father," what sort of father will listen to him? Plainly the one who is akin to the person calling, and that is not the heavenly Father but the one beneath the earth. For a person bears the marks of kinship of a particular father, and that father will surely recognize his own kin. So the prayer of a wicked man, as long as he stays in his wickedness, becomes an invocation of the devil. But the voice of one who has turned away from wickedness and lives in goodness will call upon the good Father. When we approach God, then, let us first examine our life, to see whether we carry in ourselves anything worthy of kinship with God, and only then dare to speak such a word. For the one who commanded us to say "Father" did not allow us to tell a lie. So the person who has lived in a way worthy of divine nobility rightly looks toward the heavenly city, naming the King of the heavens his Father and heavenly blessedness his fatherland. Where does the purpose of this counsel lead? To setting the mind on things above, where God is; to laying the foundations of one's dwelling there; to storing up one's treasures there; to moving one's heart there, for where the treasure is, there the heart is also; to looking always toward the Father's beauty and adorning one's own soul to match it. "There is no partiality with God," says Scripture. Let every such filth be far from your form as well. The Divine is pure of envy and of every stain of passion. Let no such passions spot you: not envy, not conceit, nor anything else that defiles the godlike beauty. If you are like this, take courage to call upon God with your own voice and to name the Master of the universe your Father. He will look on you with a father's eyes. He will clothe you in the divine robe and adorn you with the ring. He will fit your feet with the sandals of the Gospel for the journey upward, and restore you to your heavenly fatherland, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong glory and might for ages of ages. Amen. ORATION III. Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come.

The law contains the shadow of the good things to come and foretells the truth in certain typological riddles. When it brings the priest into the inner sanctuary to pray to God, it first purifies him as he enters with certain cleansings and sprinklings. Then it adorns him with the priestly robe, splendidly worked in gold and purple and the other bright colours of dye. It puts the band of the breastpiece on him, hangs the bells together with the pomegranates from the hems, binds the outer vestment above with the shoulder-pieces, and beautifies his head with the

diadem, pouring ointment generously over his hair. In this way it leads him into the sanctuary to perform the secret rites. But the spiritual Lawgiver, our Lord Jesus Christ, strips the law of its bodily veils and brings the riddles of the types into the open. First, he does not set apart one person from all the rest and lead him alone into converse with God. He grants this dignity equally to all, offering the grace of the priesthood as a common gift to all who wish for it. Next, he does not provide the priest's beauty with a borrowed adornment devised from dyes and elaborate weaving. He clothes him with an adornment that is his own and part of his nature, decking him with the graces of the virtues in place of the many-coloured purple. He adorns the breast as well, not with earthly gold, but by beautifying the loveliness of the heart with an undefiled and pure conscience. He fits into the breastpiece the gleaming of precious stones too, and these are the radiant lights of the holy commandments, as the Apostle holds. And with the undergarment he secures that part of the body for which such a garment serves as an adornment. You surely know that the covering of chastity is the adornment of that part. He also hangs the spiritual pomegranates and bells on the hems of life. One might fittingly understand these as the visible features of a virtuous way of life, which make a person's course through this life conspicuous. So from these hems he hangs the resonant word of faith in place of the bell, and in place of the pomegranate the hidden preparation of the hope to come, concealed under a more austere life. Thus he leads him into the inner, innermost sanctuary of the temple. This sanctuary is not lifeless, nor made with hands. It is the hidden storeroom of our heart, if it is truly inaccessible to evil and untrodden by wicked thoughts. He adorns the head with heavenly thinking. He does not engrave the shapes of letters on a golden plate; he stamps God himself on the ruling faculty of reason. He pours over the hair the ointment that the soul itself compounds from within through the virtues. And he prepares him to offer to God, as sacrifice and victim, through the mystical rite, nothing other than himself. Whoever is brought by the Lord into this priesthood puts to death the mind of the flesh with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. In this way, once he is in the sanctuary, he propitiates God, having offered himself in such a sacrifice and presented his own body as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God. But perhaps someone will say that the plain sense of the prayer set before us for interpretation does not contain these things. He will say we are devising ideas like these that do not suit the subject on its own terms. Then let him recall once more the first teachings of the prayer. For the one who has prepared himself in this way, so as to dare with boldness to call God his Father…

…how could any of our efforts succeed unless divine help brings about the good in us? And the sum of all good things is that the name of God should be glorified in my life. The meaning may become clearer [?] to us from its opposite. I have heard Holy Scripture somewhere condemning those who become the cause of blasphemy against God: "Woe," it says, "to those through whom my name is blasphemed among the nations." This is what it means. Those who have not yet believed in the word of truth look at the life of those who have accepted the faith of the mystery. Suppose some people bear the name of the faith, but their life contradicts that name. They worship idols through greed, or disgrace themselves in drunkenness and revelry, wallowing like pigs in the mire of debauchery. Then the unbelievers at once have a ready reproach. They do not turn the accusation against the free choice of those who have used their lives badly. They treat it as if the mystery taught people to do such things: so-and-so, who has been initiated into the divine mysteries, would not have become a slanderer, or greedy, or a robber, or anything else of the kind, unless sinning were lawful for them. That is why the Word holds out a harsh threat against such people, saying that the "Woe" belongs to those "through whom my name is blasphemed among the nations." If this has been understood, it is time to consider what is said by contrast. I think that one must pray before all else for this, and make it the heart of the prayer: that the name of God may not be blasphemed in my life, but glorified and hallowed. "In me, then," it says, "let the name of your lordship, which has been called upon me, be hallowed, so that people may see the good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven." Who is so savage and irrational as to fail to glorify it when he sees, in those who have believed in God, a pure life achieved through virtue? Such a life is clean of all the defilements of sin and far from any suspicion of evil. It is radiant with chastity and dignified in prudence. It has courage against the assaults of the passions and is never softened by bodily pleasures. It is as far as possible from luxury, indolence and the empty vanity of conceit. It shares in this life only as much as it must, touching the earth with the tip of its foot. It is not buried in this earthly life by pleasurable enjoyments, but rises above all the deception that comes through the senses and, while in the flesh, competes with the bodiless life. It considers the possession of virtue the only wealth and kinship with God the only nobility. It holds that the only dignity and the only power is to rule oneself and not be enslaved to human passions. It is weary of the long drawn-out life in this material world and hurries, like those who suffer hardship at sea, to reach the harbour

of rest. Who, then, seeing such a person, does not glorify the name that has been called upon such a life? So when someone says in prayer, "Hallowed be your name," the force of the words means he is praying for these things in himself: "With the cooperation of your help may I become blameless, just and devout. May I abstain from every evil deed, speak the truth and do what is right. May I walk in uprightness, shine with chastity and be adorned with incorruption. May I be made beautiful with wisdom and prudence, set my mind on things above, disdain earthly things, and be made radiant by an angelic way of life." These and similar things are contained in this short petition, which says to God in prayer, "Hallowed be your name." For God cannot be glorified in a human being in any other way, unless that person's virtue bears witness that the divine power is the cause of the good in him. The next phrase prays that the kingdom of God may come. Does it ask that the King of all should now become king? He always is what he is. He cannot be moved by any change, and he can find nothing better to change into. What, then, does the prayer mean when it calls for the kingdom of God? The true account of this would be known to those to whom the Spirit of truth reveals hidden mysteries. Our own understanding of the saying is this. One true authority and power stands above all things. It has taken up sovereignty over the universe and reigns, but not by any violence or tyrannical domination, as if it had yoked its subjects into submission through fear and compulsion. For virtue must be free from all fear and have no master, choosing the good by a free decision. And the sum of all good is to be placed under the life-giving authority. But human nature was led astray from its judgment of the good by deception. The inclination of our choice turned to the opposite, and human life was overpowered by everything worse, since death was decreed against our nature by countless roads. For every form of evil becomes a road for death to come against us. Since we have been held fast by such a tyranny, enslaved to death by the assaults of the passions as if by executioners or enemies, we rightly pray that the kingdom of God may come upon us. There is no other way to escape the evil domination of corruption unless the life-giving power takes over sovereignty over us in its place. So if we ask that the kingdom of God may come upon us, the force of our petition to God is this: "May I be delivered from corruption, set free from death and released from the bonds of sin. Let death no longer reign over me. Let the tyranny of evil no longer be at work against us. Let not the war overpower me or lead me captive through sin. But let your kingdom come upon me, so that the passions which now prevail and reign may withdraw from me, or rather pass away into nothing." For "as smoke vanishes, so they will vanish; and as wax melts

before the fire, so they will perish." Smoke poured out into the air leaves no trace of its own nature, and wax is no longer found once it has been in the fire. The wax feeds the flame with itself and is turned into vapour and air, and the smoke passes away until it has disappeared completely. In the same way, if the kingdom of God comes upon us, everything that now prevails will be brought to nothing. For darkness does not endure the presence of light, and disease does not hold its ground when health takes hold. The passions are powerless when freedom from passion is present. Death is gone and corruption has vanished when life reigns in us and incorruption holds sway. "Your kingdom come." How sweet these words are! Through them we bring this very petition openly before God: "Let the opposing battle line be broken. Let the phalanx of the foreigners be wiped out. Let the war of the flesh against the spirit be ended. Let the body not be a base of operations for the enemy of the soul. Let royal power appear to me, the angelic host, the thousands of those who rejoice, the myriad standing at the right hand, so that the thousand who wage war may fall on the opposing side. The adversary is great, fearsome and unconquerable to those who lack your help, but only as long as the one under attack stands alone. Once your kingdom appears, grief and groaning have fled, and life, peace and gladness come in their place." Or, as Luke explains the same idea more clearly for us, does the one who asks that the kingdom may come call for the help of the Holy Spirit? For in that Gospel, in place of "Your kingdom come," he says: "Let your Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us." What will those who speak insolently against the Holy Spirit say to this? With what reasoning do they turn the dignity of kingship into the lowliness of servitude? What Luke calls the Holy Spirit, Matthew named the kingdom. How do these fighters against God drag him down to the level of subject creation, ranking him with the nature that is ruled rather than with the nature that rules? Creation serves, and servitude is not kingship. But the Holy Spirit is kingship. So he is set apart from any common share with creation. For what reigns is not reigned over, and what is not reigned over is not creation either, since servitude is proper to creation. If the Spirit, then, is kingship, how can they refuse to confess his lordship? They have never even learned to pray. They do not even know who it is that cleanses what is defiled, or who it is on whom the authority of the kingdom depends. "Let your Holy Spirit come," it says, "and cleanse us." So the proper and special power and activity of the Holy Spirit is to cleanse and to forgive sins, as the word of the Gospel testifies. And the one who has testified that he has the power to forgive sins has surely testified to his divinity as well. The Apostle says the very same thing about

the Only-begotten: that "having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty" of the Father. The work of both, then, is one: of the Spirit, who cleanses sin, and of Christ, who made purification for sins. And where the activity is one, the power too is surely the same. For every activity is the effect of a power. If, then, activity and power are one, how can we conceive of a difference of nature in those in whom we find no difference of power and activity? Fire has two properties, giving light and burning, yet one cannot suppose that the subject they share is different [?]. In the same way, no one of sound mind who has been taught by Scripture that the Son and the Spirit have one activity would suspect any difference of nature. It has already been shown by the proofs of the pious that the nature of the Father and of the Son is the same, since things of different kinds cannot be called by the name of God [?]. In the same way, a pedestal is not called a carpenter's son, and no sensible person would say that a builder produced a son. The names "son" and "father" signify a natural bond. Necessarily, then, when two things are each akin to one and the same thing, they do not differ from each other. The Son is united to the Father by nature. And through the sameness of their activities, the Holy Spirit has been shown not to be foreign to the nature of the Son. It follows that the nature of the Holy Trinity has been shown to be one. It is not confused with respect to the property that is specially observed in each, and the distinguishing marks are not exchanged among them. What, then, is this madness of the fighters against the Spirit, who teach that the Lord is a servant? Not even Paul is believable to them when he solemnly declares, "Now the Lord is the Spirit." Or perhaps they think the words "let it come" detract from his dignity? Then do they not hear the great David drawing even the Father to himself and crying out, "Come and save us"? If coming means salvation when it is said of the Father, how can coming be a reproach when it is said of the Spirit? Or do they take cleansing from sins as a sign of lower dignity? Then listen to the unbelieving Jews crying out that forgiving sins belongs to God alone, and they were speaking of the Father: "Why does this man speak blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" The Father forgives sins. The Son takes away the sin of the world. The Holy Spirit cleanses from the defilements of sin those in whom he comes to dwell. What, then, will they say, these people who make war on their own life? But let the Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us, and make us able to receive the lofty thoughts that befit God,
which the Saviour's voice shows us through the prayer. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us today our daily bread. I once heard a physician giving an expert account of the natural basis of a healthy condition. What he said might perhaps also apply quite fittingly to the good condition of the soul. He defined the departure of any one of the elements in us from its proper measure as the beginning and cause of disease. Conversely, he said that the cure of the cause of the illness is restoring the elements that have been thrown out of tune to what is proper and natural to them. For this reason he thought one must watch, above all, for whichever element in us moves out of proportion by gaining the upper hand, and [?] make the corresponding element contribute to health. For example, if heat gains the upper hand, one should support the element being overpowered and moisten what is drying out. Otherwise, when its fuel ran out, the heat might wither away completely and be extinguished within itself, consuming itself. In the same way, if any other element among the opposites we observe in ourselves exceeds its limit, physicians should resist the excess and bring the help of their art to the one that is being diminished. When this is done, and nothing hinders the equal balance of the elements, health returns to the body, since its nature is no longer out of balance in its mixture. What, then, is the point of this long preface to my discourse? Perhaps the observation is not beside the mark, and not far removed from the subject before us. For "Your will be done" is set before us for contemplation, and we will make clear in what follows why we have recalled this medical theory. The intelligible part of the human being was once healthy. Its elements, so to speak, by which I mean the movements of the soul, were blended in us in equal balance, as virtue requires. But when the desiring part grew strong, self-control, which is understood as the disposition opposite to it, was overpowered by that excess, and nothing remained to check desire's immoderate movement toward what it should not have. From this, the deadly disease, sin, arose in human nature. So the true physician of the soul's sufferings, who came into human life for the sake of those who were ill, dissolves the cause of the disease through the thoughts contained in the prayer and leads us back to intelligible health. The health of the soul is the prospering of the divine will, just as falling away from the good will is a disease of the soul that ends in death. Since, then, we fell sick when we abandoned the good way of life in paradise, when [?] the poison of disobedience… PATROL. GR. XLIV.

[?]… and nature was overpowered by a deadly disease. Then the true Physician came, healing the evil by its opposite, as the law of medicine prescribes. Those who had fallen into the sickness because they had separated themselves from the divine will he sets free from the disease again by joining them to the will of God. For the words of the prayer are a cure for the sickness that arises in the soul. Whoever says "Your will be done" prays like someone whose soul is gripped by pain. And the will of God is the salvation of human beings. So when we come to the point of saying to God, "Let your will be done in me too," we must first of all condemn that former life which was lived outside the divine will, and [?] go through it in confession, saying: "Since the opposing will worked wickedly in me throughout my past life, and I became the servant of the evil tyrant, carrying out the enemy's [?] against myself to the very end like an executioner, take pity on my ruin, and grant that at last your will too may be done in me." For just as darkness vanishes when light is brought into gloomy caves, so when your will comes to be in me, every wicked and perverse movement of the will is reduced to nothing. Self-control will quench the mind's licentious and passionate impulse; humility will consume conceit; modesty will heal the disease of arrogance; and the good of love will drive a long list of opposing evils out of the soul. For before love there retreat hatred, envy, resentment, the angry impulse, the irritable temper, scheming, hypocrisy, the remembering of injuries, the desire to hurt back, the boiling of the blood around the heart, the bitter eye. This whole herd of evils vanishes before a loving disposition. In the same way the working of God's will drives out idolatry. I mean idolatry of two kinds: the madness for idols, and the madness for silver and gold, which the word of prophecy called the idols of the nations. So let your will be done, so that the will of the devil may be quenched. But why do we pray that the good choice should come to us from God? Because human nature is weak toward the good, having once been unstrung by vice. A person does not return from evil to the good with the same ease with which he goes to evil. The same principle can be observed in bodies: the healthy does not fall sick in the same way, or with equal ease, as the sick is made well. Someone who has been living in good health has often been brought into mortal danger by a single wound; a single bout or onset of fever has broken all the body's strength; a small taste of poison has killed outright, or very nearly; and after the bite of a snake, or the sting of some venomous creature, or a slip,

or a fall, or eating more than one can bear, or some other such thing, disease or death has followed at once. But deliverance from sickness comes only through many devices, much difficulty and the arts of medicine, if it comes at all. That is why, when our impulse is toward evil, we need no helper, for vice brings itself to completion in our will of its own accord. But if the inclination is toward the better, we need God to bring the desire into action. Therefore we say: "Since your will is self-control, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin, may this good will be accomplished in me by your power." And the same goes for righteousness, piety and detachment from the passions. For the word "will" takes in all the virtues in general, and each particular thing understood as good is seen within the will of God. But what is meant by the phrase that follows, "as in heaven, so on earth"? It seems to me that the phrase perhaps hints at some deeper doctrine, and offers a teaching worthy of God about how we should contemplate creation. What I mean is this. The whole rational creation is divided into incorporeal nature and embodied nature. The incorporeal is the angelic; the other kind is us human beings. The intelligible nature, being free of the body that weighs us down (I mean this solid body which sinks toward the earth), occupies the realm above. It dwells in light, ethereal places, and its nature is nimble and quick to move. The other nature, because our body is akin to what is earthy, like a sediment of mud, has of necessity been allotted this life on earth. I do not know what the divine will is arranging by this. Perhaps it is drawing the whole creation into kinship with itself, so that the lower realm should not lack a share in the heavenly heights, and heaven should not be wholly without a share in the things of earth. Then, through the human creature, each of the elements would share in what belongs to the other: the intellectual part of the soul, which seems to be akin to the heavenly powers and of the same race, dwells in earthly bodies, and this earthy flesh, at the restoration of all things, moves with the soul into the heavenly region. For "we shall be caught up," as the Apostle says, "in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." Whether God's wisdom arranges things in this way or in some other, the whole rational nature has been divided between these two lives. The incorporeal nature has been allotted heavenly blessedness; the other is turned toward the earth through the flesh, because of its kinship with it. Yet the desire for the beautiful and the good was built equally into both natures, and the Overseer of all made self-mastery, free will and

freedom from all necessity equal in both, so that everything honored with reason and understanding should be governed by its own independent choice. But the life above is entirely pure of vice, and nothing that belongs to the opposite side shares its commonwealth, whereas every passionate movement and disposition haunts the life below, where humanity belongs. That is why the divinely inspired word knows that the commonwealth of the holy powers in heaven is unmixed with vice and pure of every stain of sin. But all the evil that came into existence apart from the good, simply by withdrawing from it, has flowed together like dregs and mud around this low-lying life of ours. Humanity is defiled by it, and such darkness keeps it from seeing the divine light of truth. If, then, the life above is free of passion and undefiled, while the misery of life here is drenched in passions and hardships of every kind, it is clear that the commonwealth above, being pure of every evil, is established in the good will of God, since where there is no evil there must be good. Our life, on the other hand, has fallen away from its share in good things, and so has fallen away from the divine will as well. Therefore in the prayer we are taught that our life should be so cleansed of evil that, like the way of life in heaven, the will of God may govern in us too without hindrance. It is as if one were to say: "Just as your will is done among thrones and principalities and powers and dominions and every power above the world, where no vice ever obstructs the working of the good, so may the good be perfected in us too, so that, with all vice removed, your will may prosper in our souls in every respect." But suppose someone objects: "How is it possible for those allotted a life in the flesh to achieve the purity of the incorporeal powers, when the soul is sunk deep in countless cares because of the body's needs?" For this reason, it seems to me, he resolves this perplexity, and by the next phrase he [?] what seems difficult in the task set before us [?].

For I think that in these words, when he commands us to ask for our daily bread, a doctrine is set before us: that contentment with little and moderation, in keeping with freedom from passion, are put on a level with the freedom from need that belongs to the angelic nature. The angel does not ask God in prayer for a supply of bread, because he has a nature that needs no such things. But a human being was commanded to ask, because what is being emptied is always in need of what fills it up again. The constitution of human life is fluid and passing; it seeks something fresh in place of what has been used up. So whoever looks to what nature

requires, and does not drag in anything beyond what is necessary through vain cares, will not fall far short of the angelic way of life, since by his frugality he imitates in himself their freedom from need. That is why we were commanded to seek what is enough to sustain our bodily existence, saying to God, "Give bread": not luxury or wealth, not bright purple robes, not gold ornaments, not the sparkle of gems, not silver vessels, not large estates, not command of armies, not leadership in wars and over nations, not herds of horses and cattle and great flocks of other livestock, not a host of slaves, not prominence in the marketplace, not statues, not portraits, not silks, not musical performances, nor anything else of the kind that draws the soul away from the divine and more precious concern, but bread. Do you see how broad this philosophy is? How many doctrines are contained in this brief phrase? Through it he all but cries aloud to those who will listen: "Stop, you people, frittering your desires away on vain things! Stop piling up reasons for toil against yourselves! Nature's debt is small: you owe your flesh food, a modest thing and easily provided, if you look only to need. Why do you multiply the taxes you levy on yourself? For whose sake have you put yourself under the yoke of so many debts, mining silver, digging gold and [?] the gleaming stones [?]? So that this perpetual tax collector, the belly, may live in luxury through such things? But its due is bread, which fills up what the body lacks. Yet you trade with the Indians, risk the barbarian sea and give yourself up to year-long voyages, so that you can season your food with the imports from there, without considering that the sensation of seasonings stops at the palate. In the same way, what looks fine, smells sweet and tastes good gives the senses a short-lived and momentary pleasure; past the palate there is no telling apart what has been put in, since nature turns everything alike into foulness. Do you see where [?] ends? Do you see what the sorcery of cookery comes to? Ask for bread for the needs of life; this is what nature has made you owe the body. Everything else invented by the contrivances of the luxurious belongs to the tares sown among the wheat. The householder's seed is the wheat, and bread comes from wheat; but luxury is the tare sown among the wheat by the enemy." But people neglect to serve nature with what is necessary. They are truly choked, as the Word says, by their eagerness for vain things, and they remain unfruitful, because the soul keeps itself constantly busy with these things.

It seems to me that Moses too may be teaching something of this sort in riddles, when he presents the serpent to Eve as the counselor of the pleasure of taste. For they say that if this creature, the serpent, gets its head into a crevice and slips inside, it cannot easily be pulled out by the tail by those trying to drag it back, because the scales along its spine naturally resist in the opposite direction against the force of those pulling. Its way forward is unhindered, since the smooth scales slide along, but pulling it back out is impossible, because the edges of the scales catch and hold it. By this, I think, the word shows that we must guard against pleasure entering and slipping into the crevices of the soul, and must block up the joints of our life as tightly as we can. In this way human life would be kept pure of any mingling with the beasts. But if the serpent of pleasure finds some [?] from us, because the harmony of our life has been loosened, it will make its den in us through these openings, and because of its scales it becomes hard to drive out of the recesses of the mind. When you hear "scales," understand by the riddle the many and varied occasions of pleasure. Taken as a class, the passion of pleasure is a single beast; but the varied and manifold [?] of pleasures, which have mingled with human life through the senses, are the scales on the serpent, spotted with the variety of the passions. So if you would avoid living with the beast, watch out for its head, [?] the first assault of evil. This is what the riddle of the Lord's command points to: "He shall watch for your heel, and you shall watch for his head." Do not let the creeper find a way in as it crawls toward the inner [?], drawing its whole length in after it from the first beginning. Keep to what you need: let the limit of your concern for living be the filling of what is lacking with whatever comes to hand. But if Eve's counselor should also talk to you about what is beautiful to look at and pleasant to taste, and you start looking for such and such a dish to go with your bread, prepared with such and such seasonings, and through these things you lead your desire beyond the limits of necessity, then you will see the creeper stealthily crawling on, step by step, toward greed. Having crept from necessary food to gourmandizing, it will move on to what pleases the eyes, seeking splendid dishes, delicate servants and silver couches. (Gen. 3:[?])

[?] from surfeit it is dragged down, writhing, into unbridled frenzy, and this is the worst of human evils. So that none of this may happen, set a limit to your life with a sufficiency of bread, and look for the relish that nature itself prepares for you. Above all, that relish is a good conscience, which makes bread sweet when it is honestly come by. And if you also want the sense in your throat to be pleased, let want be your relish. Do not heap surfeit on surfeit, and do not dull your appetite with drunkenness; let the sweat of the commandments come before your food: "In sweat and toil you shall eat your bread." There you see the Word's first recipe. It is enough for you to occupy your mind up to the point of this need; or rather, [do not] bind your soul with cares about bread even to that extent. Instead, say to the one who brings bread out of the earth, say to the one who feeds the ravens, who gives food to all flesh, who opens his hand and fills every living thing with his good pleasure: "My life is from you; let the means of life also come from you. Give me bread; that is, let me have food from honest labor." For if God is righteousness, the one whose food comes from greed does not have his bread from God. You yourself are master of your prayer. If your plenty does not come from what belongs to others, if your income does not come from tears, if no one has gone hungry so that you could be full, if no one has groaned so that you could have your fill, then such bread is above all God's: the fruit of righteousness, the ear of grain of peace, unmixed and undefiled by the seeds of tares. But if you farm what belongs to others, keep injustice always before your eyes, secure your unjust possessions with legal documents, and then say to God, "Give bread," then the one who hears this voice of yours is someone else, not God. The fruit of injustice is borne by the opposing nature. Whoever strives for righteousness receives bread from God; whoever cultivates injustice is fed by the benefactor of injustice. So look to your own conscience when you bring your request for bread to God, knowing that there is no fellowship between Christ and Belial. Even if you bring offerings from injustice, the gift is the price of a dog and the wages of a prostitute. And even if you make your donations splendid with lavish display, you will hear the Prophet loathing contributions of that kind: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full of whole burnt offerings of rams; I do not want the fat of lambs or the blood of bulls and goats. Incense," he says, "is an abomination to me." Elsewhere he counts the one who sacrifices a calf as no better than one who kills a dog. If, then, you have your bread from the Lord, that is, from honest labor, you may also offer him first fruits from the fruits of righteousness.

[?] toward the more divine, laying down the law that those who approach God become gods? "Why," he says, "do you approach God like a slave, cowering in fear and whipped by your own conscience? Why do you shut yourself out of the freedom of speech that belongs to the freedom of the soul, which was part of your nature from the beginning? Why do you flatter with words the One who cannot be flattered? Why do you offer servile, fawning words to the One who looks at deeds? You may have every good thing that comes from God as your own by right, with a free spirit. Be your own judge; pass the saving verdict on yourself. You ask God to forgive your debts: forgive, and God has already decreed it. The judgment about your fellow man, of which you are master, becomes an equal verdict for you, whatever it may be. For whatever you decide in your own case is confirmed for you by the divine judgment." But how could anyone unveil worthily the grandeur of the divine utterance? The saying is beyond what words can explain: "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." What occurs to me to think about it is daring even to grasp with the mind, and daring too to reveal in speech. For what is being said? God is set before those who do good as a model to imitate, as the Apostle said: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." In the same way, but in reverse, he wants your disposition to become a model of the good for God. The order is in a sense turned around. Just as good is accomplished in us by imitating the Divine, so we may dare to hope that God imitates what is ours whenever we accomplish something good. Then you too can say to God: "What I have done, do. Imitate your servant, O Lord, the poor and needy man, you who reign over all. I have forgiven debts; do not reject your suppliant. I sent my debtor away cheerful; let yours go away the same. Do not make your debtor gloomier than mine. Let the two of them give thanks alike to their creditors; let forgiveness be confirmed alike by both of us to our debtors, mine and yours. My debtor is so-and-so, and yours is me. Let the decision I made about him prevail with you. I released; release. I forgave; forgive. I showed great mercy to my fellow man; imitate the kindness of your servant, O Lord." "But my offenses against you are heavier than what this man has done against me." I say so too. But consider this as well: how far you surpass us in every good. It is right for you to grant us sinners mercy in proportion to the greatness of your power. I showed only a little kindness, because my nature could not hold more.

…but you, as much as you wish: his power does not hold back his generosity. But let us examine more thoroughly [?] the phrase of the prayer before us, in case contemplating its meaning may also give us some guidance toward the lofty life. Let us then look into which things human nature is liable for, and which, in turn, are those of which we are masters by our own choice. From knowing these we might gain some modest understanding of how far the divine goods surpass us. So let us begin here by listing humanity's offenses against God. The first penalty that man incurred toward God was for removing himself from his Maker and deserting to the adversary, becoming a runaway from his natural Master and a rebel. The second was for exchanging his free self-determination for the wicked slavery of sin, and preferring to be tyrannized by the destroying power over being with God. And again, not to look toward the beauty of the One who made him, but to turn his face toward the ugliness of sin: what evil would this be judged second to? And contempt for the divine goods, and preference for the baits of the evil one: in what class of punishment would that be ranked? And the effacing of the image, the defiling of the divine stamp that was formed in us at the first creation, the loss of the coin, the departure from the father's table, the familiarity with the foul-smelling life of the swine, the squandering of the precious wealth, and all such offenses as can be seen both in Scripture and by reasoning: what account could count them all? Since, then, humanity is liable to God for such things and owes Him the payment of penalties, the Word seems to me, in its teaching on prayer, to instruct us never to speak boldly in our petition to God as though our conscience were pure, even if someone is as far removed as possible from human offenses. For perhaps someone, like that young man of many possessions, has trained his life by the commandments and has something of this kind to boast of in his own life, and can say to God, "All these I have kept from my youth." He may suppose that, because he has transgressed none of the commandments, the plea for release from debts hardly suits him, since it suits only those who have sinned. Such words, he says, befit the man defiled by fornication; the request for pardon is necessary for the man who has committed idolatry through covetousness; and for anyone at all who has branded the [?] of his soul with some offense it is right and fitting to take refuge in mercy. But if it were that great Elijah, or the one who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, the greatest among those born of women, or Peter, or Paul, or John, or anyone else of those whom divine Scripture attests

as excellent, what use would such a person have for words like these, which beg to be let off debts, when he owes [?] nothing because of sin? The answer is that no one should look at such things and grow arrogant like that Pharisee, who did not recognize what he was by nature. For if he had known that he was a man, he would surely have learned from holy Scripture that our nature is not clean of filth, where it says that it is impossible for a man to live a single day without [?] being found in him. So that nothing of the kind may arise in the soul of one who approaches God in prayer, the Word urges us not to look at our achievements.
