Instead we are to recall the common debts of human nature, which each of us surely shares, since each shares in that nature, and to beseech the Judge to grant an amnesty for our offenses. For Adam lives in us, in every one of us individually, so long as we see these garments of skin about our nature, and the transient leaves of this material life. Stripped of our own bright garments, we stitched these leaves together for ourselves to our harm, putting on luxuries and glories, fleeting honors and the short-lived gratifications of the flesh in place of the divine robes. He lives in us so long as we look upon the place of [?] where we were condemned to dwell. Whenever we turn ourselves toward the east, it is not as though God were seen only there, for He who is everywhere is not grasped in any particular part, since He holds the whole equally in His embrace. We turn there because our first homeland lies in the east: I mean the life in paradise from which we have fallen, for "God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east." When, then, we look toward the east and call to mind how we fell from the luminous eastern place of blessedness, we rightly put forward such a cry. We are shaded by the wicked fig tree of this life, cast out from the sight of God. We have deserted to the serpent, which eats earth, crawls on the ground and goes on its breast and belly, and advises us to do the same: to be occupied with earthly enjoyment, to drag our hearts along in groveling, earthbound thoughts, and to go upon our belly, that is, to busy ourselves with the life of pleasure. In this condition we are like that prodigal after the long misery he endured feeding the swine. When we come to ourselves as he did and call the heavenly Father to mind, we do well to use such words as "Forgive us our debts." So even someone like Moses, or Samuel, or anyone else outstanding in virtue considers this cry no less fitting for himself, inasmuch as he is a man. For he shares the nature of Adam, and so he shares also in Adam's fall. [?]

For since, as the Apostle says, "in Adam we all die," it is fitting that all who died with Adam should use the words that suited Adam's repentance. Then, once we have been granted amnesty for our offenses, we may be saved again by grace from the Lord, as the Apostle says. But all this has been said so that one might view the passage before us in its more general sense. If one seeks the true meaning of the saying, I do not think we need to refer it to what is common to our nature, for each person's conscience, from the life he has lived, is enough to make the request for mercy necessary. Life operates in us in many forms in this world, partly in the soul and mind and partly in the senses of the body. It is therefore difficult, or rather altogether impossible, not to be carried into sin by some passion. I mean something like this. The pleasure-seeking life of the body is divided among our senses, while the life of the soul is seen in the impulse of the mind and the movement of choice. Who, then, is so lofty and so great of spirit as to stay free of the defilement of vice in both? Who is sinless with the eye? Who is blameless in what he hears? Who is a stranger to this beastly pleasure of the throat? Who is clean in touch from the grip of sin? Who does not know the riddle of Scripture, which says, "Death has come in through the windows"? The senses, through which the soul goes out to external things and takes hold of what it desires, are what Scripture has called windows, and the Word says that they open the way for death to enter. And truly the eye often becomes the entrance of many deaths. It sees someone angry and is roused in turn to the same passion. It sees someone prospering beyond his deserts and is inflamed with envy. It sees someone arrogant and falls into hatred. Or it sees some brightly colored material, or a more beautifully shaped form, and slides wholly into desire for what pleased it. In the same way the ear opens the windows to death: through what it hears it lets many passions into the soul, such as fear, grief, anger, pleasure, desire, bursts of laughter and the like. As for the enjoyment that comes through taste, one might call it the mother of every single evil. For who does not know that preoccupation with the throat is close to being the root of the offenses of life? On it depend luxury, drunkenness, gluttony, wastefulness in diet, surfeit, satiety, revelry, and the brutish, irrational plunge into dishonorable passions. Likewise the sense of touch is the furthest extreme of all sins. For everything that lovers of pleasure practise with the body is a disease of the faculty of touch. It would take too long to describe these one by one, and it is not fitting to mix the charges that belong to touch with more dignified discourse.

And who could count the swarm of offenses committed in the soul and the will? "From within," he says, "come evil thoughts"; and he added a list of the thoughts that defile us. If, then, the nets of sin are cast around us on every side in this way, through all the sense organs and through the movements of the soul within the heart, who will boast, as Wisdom says, of having a pure heart? Who is cleansed from filth, as Job testifies? The filth that stains the purity of the soul is pleasure, which mixes itself into human life in many parts and many ways: through soul and body, through thoughts, through the senses, through the movements of the will, through bodily acts. Who, then, has a soul pure of this stain? Who has not been struck by conceit? Who has not been trampled by the foot of pride? Whom has the sinner's hand not shaken? Whose foot has not run toward evil? Who has not been stained by an unruly eye or soiled by an undisciplined ear? Whom has taste not occupied with itself? Whose heart has stayed idle toward vain impulses? Our condition is worse and harder in the more brutish. But in every way and without exception, all who share the nature also share in the offenses of the nature. That is why we fall down before God in prayer and beseech Him to forgive us our debts. Yet such a cry achieves nothing, even if it reaches divine ears, unless our conscience cries out with us that showing mercy is good. Whoever judges that kindness befits God must think it fitting, for he would not ask God to do what is unbecoming and unsuitable. It is only just, then, that he should confirm by his own deeds his judgment about what is good. Otherwise he may hear something like this from the Judge: "Physician, heal yourself. You call on me for kindness, which you yourself have not shown to your neighbors? You ask for the forgiveness of debts; how, then, do you throttle your debtor? You pray that the bond against you be blotted out, while you carefully keep the contracts of those who owe you. You ask for debts to be cancelled, while you fatten the loan with interest. Your debtor is in prison and you are in the house of prayer. He is in anguish over his debts, and you ask that your own debt be forgiven you. Your prayer goes unheard, for the voice of the one in anguish drowns it out. If you release the bodily debt, the bonds of your soul will be released. If you forgive, you will be forgiven. You will judge yourself and make the law for yourself: your attitude toward the one beneath you will bring the verdict from above upon your own head." The Lord seems to me to teach something of this kind in another passage as well,

where He sets out this teaching as a story. In the story there is a king, presiding in fearsome majesty, who brings his servants to judgment and demands an account of what each has managed. One of the debtors is brought before him and obtains kindness, because he falls down and offers supplication instead of paying the money. Then he treats his fellow servant bitterly and harshly over a modest debt. His harshness toward his fellow servant angers the king, who orders the torturers to banish him entirely from the king's house and to keep up the punishment until he has paid the full penalty he deserves. For truly, the debts our brothers owe us, compared with our offenses against God, are like a few paltry, easily counted obols set beside tens of thousands of talents. Suppose someone has done you damage or given you cause to feel insulted, or a servant has done wrong, or there has even been a plot against your bodily life. Then you are provoked to revenge with an inflamed heart, and search out every device for punishing those who have grieved you. If your anger is inflamed against a servant, do you not consider that it was not nature but power that divided humanity into slavery and lordship? For the Steward of the universe ordained that only irrational nature should serve man, as the Prophet says: "You have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, the birds and the beasts and the fish." Elsewhere prophecy even calls these slaves, when it says, "giving the beasts their food, and grass for the service of men." But man He adorned with the grace of free will. So the one bound under you by custom and law is your equal in the dignity of nature. He did not come into being from you, he does not live in you, and he did not receive from you the bodily and mental activities of his soul. Why, then, do you boil over with such anger against him if he has been negligent, or has run away, or has perhaps shown you contempt to your face? Should you not look at yourself, and at what kind of servant you have been to the Master who formed you, brought you into being through birth, and made you a sharer in the wonders of the world? He set the sun before you for your enjoyment and granted you all the means of life from the elements: from earth and fire, air and water. He gave you the gift of intellect, perceiving sense, and the knowledge that distinguishes good from worse. How will you prove obedient and blameless toward such a Master? Did you not desert His lordship? Did you not run away to sin? Did you not exchange it for a wicked lordship? Did you not, as far as it lay with you, leave the Master's house deserted, the house in which you were appointed to work and to keep it, and run away from it? And the offenses I have listed: is God not witness, He who is [?] everywhere and watches over all things, when you do

or say or think what you ought not? Then, being such a one and owing so much, do you think you are doing your fellow servant some great favor if you overlook an offense he has committed against you? If, then, we mean to bring before God our plea for mercy and pardon, let us give our conscience grounds for boldness, so that we may put forward our life as advocate for this cry and say truly: "As we also have forgiven our debtors." What do the words that follow mean? I think it necessary not to pass over these unexamined either, so that we may know what we are praying for and offer our supplication with the soul [?] and not with the body [?]: "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." What, brothers, is the force of these words? The Lord seems to me to name the evil one in many and various ways, calling him by many names according to the different kinds of his wicked activity: devil, Beelzebul, Mammon, ruler of the world, murderer, evil one, father of lies, and so on. Perhaps, then, "temptation" is also one of the names applied to him, and the structure of the words confirms this suspicion. For having said, "Lead us not into temptation," He added "deliver us from the evil one," as though both names signified the same thing. If one who has not entered into temptation is entirely outside the evil one, and one who has come into temptation is necessarily in the evil one, then temptation and the evil one mean one and the same thing. What, then, does this teaching on prayer command us to do? To be outside the things that are seen in this world. As He says elsewhere to the disciples, "the whole world lies in the evil one." So whoever wishes to be outside the evil one will necessarily remove himself from the world. For temptation has no means of touching the soul unless it holds out this worldly preoccupation to the greedier sort, like bait on the evil hook. Perhaps the thought would become clearer to us through other examples. The sea is often dangerous because of great waves, but not to those who live far away from it. Fire is destructive, but only to the material that falls into it. War is terrible, but only to those who take part in the battle. The man who wants to escape the calamities of war prays not to fall into war. The man who fears fire prays not to be in it. The man who dreads the sea prays not to be forced into a voyage. In the same way, let the man who fears the assault of the evil one pray not to be in him. And since, as we said before, the Word says that the world lies in the evil one, and the occasions of temptation lie in worldly affairs, the one who prays to be delivered from the evil

one is fittingly and aptly asking to be outside temptations. For no one would swallow the hook without first greedily gulping down the bait. So let us also rise and say to God, "Lead us not into temptation" (that is, into the evils of life), "but deliver us from the evil one," who holds power in this world. May we be delivered from him by the grace of Christ, for to Him belong the power and the glory, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
